hints: Focus on what excess chlorine with UV light means, free radical substitution can keep replacing H atoms until none are left.
List the possible molecular formulas from one Cl up to six Cls, that is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ through to $\text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$.
Now count structural isomers for each formula by moving the Cl atoms between the 1,1 and 1,2 positions, then add them all together.
walkthrough:
**Understand the reaction conditions**

Think like a teacher with you. UV light starts free radical substitution of H by Cl.

Excess chlorine means the reaction does not stop at one Cl. It goes all the way to:
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \rightarrow ... \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$$

**List every formula that still has two carbons**

We only count products with two C atoms and at least one Cl. That gives six formulas:
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}, \text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Cl}_2, \text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{Cl}_3, \text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{Cl}_4, \text{C}_2\text{HCl}_5, \text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$$

**Count structural isomers for each formula**

This is the key skill. Draw the Cl atoms on C1 and C2:

$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$: 1 isomer, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$

$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Cl}_2$: 2 isomers, 1,1- ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHCl}_2$) and 1,2- ($\text{CH}_2\text{ClCH}_2\text{Cl}$)

$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{Cl}_3$: 2 isomers, 1,1,1- ($\text{CH}_3\text{CCl}_3$) and 1,1,2- ($\text{CHCl}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$)

$\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{Cl}_4$: 2 isomers, 1,1,1,2- ($\text{CH}_2\text{ClCCl}_3$) and 1,1,2,2- ($\text{CHCl}_2\text{CHCl}_2$)

**Finish the count and conclude**

$\text{C}_2\text{HCl}_5$: 1 isomer, $\text{CHCl}_2\text{CCl}_3$ only, swapping carbons gives the same molecule.

$\text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$: 1 isomer, $\text{CCl}_3\text{CCl}_3$ only.

Add them: $1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 9$ different products.

options.A: 8 is one too few. It usually comes from missing one isomer, most often forgetting that $\text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$ counts even though it has no H, or thinking the two $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{Cl}_4$ isomers are the same.
options.B: 9 is correct. The full count is 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 9 structural isomers from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ to $\text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$.
options.C: 10 is one too many. It often comes from inventing a stereoisomer or counting the same structure twice, for example thinking $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{ClCH}_3$ are different. Rotation about the C-C single bond does not create new isomers here.
options.D: 12 is far too high. It often comes from guessing 6 formulas times 2 isomers each, but the end members $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, $\text{C}_2\text{HCl}_5$ and $\text{C}_2\text{Cl}_6$ each have only 1 isomer.
